Hi,
I'm writing because in our research we are having some problems. We are using an advanced sleeplog, which includes: hour woke up and went to bed and includes nap time with the same information. It is because we are working with people who haven't a regular timetable. When we analyze the sleeplog whit Ggir an error occurs and it don't bring us a result, despite the software doesn't notify any error. We wonder if the sleeplog is the problem or if we have to change some part of the code in the program.
In any case, thank you for reading and hope someone could help

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] default physical activity threshold values
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] default physical activity threshold values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lena,

Some of the thresholds were chosen because they were considered sufficient in one specific study I worked on at the time when I wrote the code. They are not intended to be a recommendation for all use cases.

Sometimes we may want to round or average multiple thresholds proposed in papers to avoid the impression of extreme precession. They are not much more than a crude way to segment behaviour in intensity levels.

Further, once a default argument value has been set it is common practise in software to never change the default unless there is convincing evidence that a different default is better. This to support reproducibility. We know that there is no universally applicable optimal threshold combination, by which any default is by definition flawed. I think each user will have to decide for themselves what thresholds to use.

Thanks,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

The main approaches I can think of are:

Focus on the day- and/or night- summary csv reports and to generate your own aggregates for each time point.
Load the part 1 milestone file (RData in meta/basci), split it in two, and save each part as a new part 1 milestone file. The key here is to split the M$metashort and M$metalong objects. Next, you should be able to process it with the other GGIR parts as if it were two separate recordings.

For either approach you will need to write some custom code as GGIR does not facilitate this kind of splitting yet. I deprecated the selectdaysfile option because it was entirely written to only work with 2 days only, which I think was too specific and it caused a lot of maintenance effort.  Let me know if you are interested in helping to enhance GGIR to facilitate data collection protocols like this in a more flexible and sustainable way compared with what selectdaysfile used to do.

Best regards,

Vincent

4. Could it be that memory per process is unusually low on your machine that this somehow kills or interrupts the parallel jobs? I have to say that GGIR does not monitor that in high detail but assumes that process has roughly 2 GB available (e.g. 16 GB RAM on 8 core laptop). If this would be an issue then maybe test chunksize = 0.4 which reduce the memory needs of GGIR per process. If this solves the difference then that would indicate that GGIR needs to be improved to monitor available memory and data loss in more detail.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

First of all, many thanks for a quick response! It did indeed help me locate the problem, which seems to be related to how file names are stored in g.part1, rather than the processing itself.

I am using a set of self-made functions (packaged, as for now, mostly for my own use, as https://github.com/lebatsnok/afterGGIR) to facilitate my workflow with GGIR. One of these functions reads in the .RData files in GGIR output, among these the files in "results/output_XYZ/meta/basic", and uses the variable called filename_dir as a starting point to find out the subject ID (coded into the file name). It appears (if I'm not mistaken) that this variable is occasionally wrong if there are many files in the source folder.

The following code demonstrates what I think to be a bug (probably irrelevant  to most users, though):

get.id.from.file <- function(fn) sub("Subject Code:", "", readLines(fn, 39, skipNul=TRUE)[39])
get.id.from.ggir.results <- function(fn) Load(paste0("results/output_", dirname(fn), "/meta/basic/meta_", basename(fn), ".RData"))$filename_dir
# `Load` (source at the end of this email or in lebatsnok/afterGGIR) loads everything from an
# Rdata file into a temporary environment, converts this into a list and returns this list
# (leaving the global environment unchanged!)

processed_files <- paste0("bin/", sub(".RData$", "", sub("meta_", "", dir("results/output_bin/meta/basic"))))

id1 <- sapply(processed_files, get.id.from.file)
id2 <- sapply(processed_files, get.id.from.ggir.results)
id3 <- sapply(strsplit(basename(id2), "_"), head, 1)

df <- data.frame(filename = processed_files, bin.id <http://bin.id> = id1, ggir.id <http://ggir.id> = id3, ggir.fn = id2)
rownames(df) <- NULL

openxlsx::write.xlsx(df, "df.xlsx") ## the result is attached

In this table, the participant's ID code appears in three columns:

1) File name (column A)
2) "Subject Code:" - 39th row in bin file (column B, always identical to the ID in column A)
3) "ggir.fn" -  the filename_dir variable from .RData file in meta/basic directory (column D)
4) "ggir.id <http://ggir.id>" - the ID component extracted from the filename (as recorded in filename_dir variable, column C)

In the original data folder, there are 2 bin files that did not produce output, one of them (ID=1750) containing no data (2KB, 64 header rows in the bin file, probably something happened during download, which we haven't yet checked) - and the discrepancy appears right after that file. That is, for the first 35 files, file name in `filename_dir` in meta/basic/*.RData is correct, and for the remaining files, it refers to the preceding file.

I believe I can now solve my problem (using the actual filename instead  of filename_dir variable) but the part in GGIR part 1 code that produces filename_dir may be worth checking.

Best regards,
Kenn

Load <- function (file, to.list = TRUE, Unlist = TRUE, spray = FALSE,
    delete.parent = FALSE, Attach = FALSE)
{
    attachYN <- (is.logical(Attach) & isTRUE(Attach)) | is.character(Attach)
    if (attachYN) {
        attachNAME <- if (is.logical(Attach))
            date()
        else Attach[1]
    }
    NE <- if (spray)
        .GlobalEnv
    else if (attachYN)
        attach(NULL, name = attachNAME)
    else new.env()
    load(file, NE)
    if (attachYN)
        return(invisible(NULL))
    if (to.list) {
        NE <- as.list(NE)
        if (Unlist & length(NE) == 1)
            NE <- NE[[1]]
    }
    if (delete.parent)
        parent.env(NE) <- emptyenv()
    NE
}

Instead GGIR uses the name of the underlying accelerometer file inside the name of the RData file, and that is what GGIR across GGIR to keep track of the different files. This process should be unaffected by parallel versus non-parallel processing.

Conclusions/Action points:
Do not trust filename_dir. Instead use the filename incorreported in the name of the RData file.
We will have to fix or deprecate object filename_dir. I have created an issue for this: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/issues/721#issuecomment-1359770041
It looks like this segment of the GGIR code could benefit from some cleaning up work more generally as it seems old and not clearly written.

Dear Gengze,

Your code looks good. By specifying argument includenightcrit = 16​ you ask GGIR to only estimate sleep from nights with at least 16 hours of data between noon and the following noon (if the person wakes up after noon then the window is defined between 6pm and 6pm).

Your pdf visualisations indicates your recordings started after 6pm, which makes it impossible for GGIR to find 16 or more valid hours before the next noon.

One solution is that you lower the value for includenightcrit​ to for example 14, although that could compromise the reliability of estimates for other recording.

A better but less quick solution is that we develop an enhancement of GGIR to consider a late start of the recording when trying to detect sleep for the first night. Here, I see the following options:
You or someone else develops this as a contribution to GGIR.
You or someone else hires me to develop this.
I keep put it on my list of ideas for the future and maybe at some point in the upcoming year(s) I can do the work as part of another project.

Best regards,

Vincent

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Over or underestimation of sedentary behavior
messages.body_plain:
Dear Iris,

I see you chose a moderate threshold of 69 with a 1 minute epoch without considering consider bouts. The possible explanations that may be worth investigating:
Threshold choice in relation to wear location and age group: I am guessing you are working with hip data, correct? If not, how did you arrive at this threshold? If yes, then I suppose what you do is in line with literature for adult populations https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/CutPoints.html
Calibration of the data: Should not be a problem if you have several days of data with good compliance. See part2_summary variable calib_err, if this is below 0.005 then it should be good.
Choice of metric in relation to wear location. Metric ENMO has primarily been motivated for studies with wrist-worn sensors. It may be worth trying out the MAD metric (see cut-points Vähä-Ypyä 2015).
Discrepancy with analytical approach by Actilife setting used. If you used Actilife to classify behaviour based on shorter epochs then I would expect that to result in more active time. If Actilife was used with some kind of bout or sojourn detection algorithm then I would expect it to result in lest active time.
Mix-up of participant IDs. Double check that start date makes sense and is consistent between Actilife and GGIR. Ideally we never make these kind of mistakes, but can be good to double check.

Kind regards,

Vincent
